Brahman is the ultimate, transcendent reality at the heart of Hindu metaphysics. It is the infinite, formless, eternal principle that underlies and permeates all existence. Unlike Brahma, the creator deity, Brahman is the impersonal, non-dual cosmic principle from which all being emerges and to which all consciousness returns. The realization of Brahman and its identity with one's own innermost self, called atman, is the ultimate spiritual goal in Hinduism. In the Upanishads, Brahman is described as sat-chit-ananda, meaning being, consciousness, and bliss—the unchanging essence underlying the changing phenomenal world. The concept represents non-duality, or Advaita, the philosophical position that apparent multiplicity masks an underlying unified reality. Brahman cannot be directly described or fully comprehended by language or thought; it can only be realized through direct mystical experience, or moksha. The famous Upanishadic teaching "tat tvam asi" asserts the identity between Brahman and atman, the individual soul. Brahman is beyond all qualities, attributes, and gender. The personal gods of Hinduism—Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva—are understood as manifestations or aspects of Brahman. Liberation, or moksha, in Hindu philosophy consists of realizing one's fundamental identity with Brahman and escaping the cycle of rebirth.
